item.title: An Airbag of Loving Aunties: Reflections on Gratitude
item.description:
Gratitude

An Airbag of Loving Aunties: Reflections on Gratitude

Personal Perspective: What gratitude made room for after a crash.

Posted September 25, 2026

Key points
  • Regular gratitude practice may influence what we notice later.
  • In some studies the effects of gratitude were measurable months later.
  • Thankfulness can sit comfortably alongside disruption and uncertainty.
Kindness at the roadside
Source: Merve Arli / Pexels

A few hours before I crashed my car, I was horizontal on the floor of a friend's house being purified by fire. At least, that was what the card I'd drawn from her card deck suggested.

My friend had invited six of us to a sound bath, creating one of those safe, non-judgmental spaces where it feels easy to relax and let go. As she moved around us with her Tibetan bowls, I felt something begin to course through me.

It wasn't the soft golden light I'd vaguely expected. It felt more like fire, raw and cleansing, like a swift river of lava. Giving up on the soft tinkly bells I thought I'd signed up for, I surrendered to it and set an intention: to let anything that was out of alignment with the person I was becoming be swept away.

With hindsight, maybe I shouldn't have done that.

Afterwards, I drove to the beach. It felt important to plant my feet in the sand. I had one of those strict conversations with myself, as you do. Paraphrasing here: "Life has to change. The way I’m showing up isn’t working out so well."

Then I remembered a gratitude practice that I’d developed some time ago, a sequence I used to practice every day. It had helped me through a difficult period many years earlier when my life was changing profoundly. The present moment felt strangely similar, so I started talking to myself, out loud. Of course I pretended to be on my phone so nobody called the police.

What followed was a twenty-minute monologue praising the trees, the beach, and the silvery sky. And then I turned the corner and spied my beautiful, sleek, fat-bottomed Audi TT hugging the ground, waiting for me to climb in for our next adventure. She positively glowed with mischief.

Driving home through my neighborhood, I was still flooded with appreciation. In my imagination this feeling was spilling out of the car, blessing everyone on Main Street and circling the golfers on the hill.

Then, whack!

I watched, almost in slow motion, as the front of my beautiful car sailed into the air. My first thought was surprisingly prosaic: That could be expensive.

The vehicle that had hit me careened across the road. I remember tracking it, wrapping the driver in thoughts of protection and, at the same time, having a strange certainty that we would both be OK. Thankfully, we were. And then came the part I still find interesting.

I remember feeling no stress or panic, just deep, soft gratitude.

This wasn’t the type of thankfulness you manufacture because you've read somewhere that it’s good for you. I wasn't sitting inside my wrecked car dutifully trying to think of three things I was grateful for. It was simply there, the backdrop to my experience. It was as if I'd been cushioned by an airbag of loving aunties.

The other driver was shaken and furious. I got out calmly and started clearing pieces of car from the road. One man whistled cheerfully while dodging traffic and sweeping debris from the road. Someone taped up the sad little dribble coming from my burst radiator. Then a woman materialized, almost genie-like, carrying a hot, sweet cup of tea and a notepad.

“How very British,” I remember thinking, having lived abroad for several years.

The insurance company was kind, and the recovery teams were considerate. Everyone seemed to want to help. It began to feel as though we'd all joined some strange conspiracy.

What do we practice when nothing is wrong?

Over the next few days, the gratitude didn't diminish, and friends commented on how calmly I seemed to be dealing with the disruption. Some wondered whether I was in shock, but I just felt unusually present.

We tend to think of gratitude as a response to circumstances; something good happens and we feel grateful. But could practicing gratitude repeatedly change what becomes easier for us to notice later? I got curious and started researching.

In one randomized study, people entering psychotherapy for depression or anxiety were assigned to either therapy alone, therapy with expressive writing, or therapy with gratitude writing. Three months later, those in the gratitude-writing group showed more gratitude in their behavior and greater neural sensitivity to gratitude in the medial prefrontal cortex. The researchers suggested that the effects of the exercise might last beyond the writing itself.

More recent research found that while a five-minute gratitude exercise didn't significantly change participants' positive memory bias, those who recorded a grateful event every day for two months subsequently showed greater positive memory bias than a control group.

The evidence is preliminary, and none of this proves that years of rehearsing gratitude caused my unusual response to the accident, but it did make me question why gratefulness was so readily available to me at a moment when I might reasonably have felt anything but it.

My car was badly damaged, and there was inconvenience and uncertainty. Gratitude didn't make any of that disappear, but I didn't have to go looking for what was good. I could still appreciate the damaged car and the intact bodies, the furious driver and the whistling stranger who helped me sweep the street. And I will never forget the woman who emerged from a house nearby carrying the hot, sweet tea.

The Audi was eventually written off, so there wasn't even a happy ending, and I’m looking for a new adventure partner now, but what surprised me most about the accident wasn't the crash or the aftermath. It was discovering that when everything went wrong, I didn't have to remind myself to be grateful because I already was.

item.title: Are We Misreading Autistic Empathy Expressions?
item.description:
Autism

Are We Misreading Autistic Empathy Expressions?

When care doesn’t look the way we expect it to.

Posted September 25, 2026

Key points
  • Cultural norms influence what we recognize as empathy.
  • When autistic people show care in ways that differ from cultural conventions, we may misinterpret it.
  • Some autistic people express care through problem-solving, sharing a similar experience, or being direct.
  • Asking what someone meant before drawing conclusions can help avoid misunderstandings.
Roses in yellow and pink
Source: enkuu smile / Unsplash

This article was written in collaboration with Tristan Lavender.

Most Western cultures teach specific rules for expressing empathy. Do these sound familiar? Don’t try to fix the problem. Don’t offer advice. Don’t respond to someone’s story with a similar story of your own. Instead, listen and stay with the other person’s experience. Active listening guidance sometimes teaches these rules explicitly (University of Iowa, n.d.).

That can be helpful advice. But when we treat empathy as something that can only be expressed according to a fixed set of rules, we leave no room for people who convey care and concern differently. For autistic people specifically, that means having their ways of expressing empathy misread or dismissed.

Empathy Is Culturally Shaped

Cultural psychology has clearly established that perceptions and expected forms of caring vary across cultures. In one study, European Americans reported providing more emotion-focused than problem-focused support, while Japanese participants showed exactly the opposite (Chen et al., 2012). Research has also distinguished explicit support, such as seeking advice and emotional comfort, from implicit support, such as finding relief in the fact of connection to valued social groups. In one series of studies, Asian and Asian-American study participants benefited more from implicit support, while European Americans benefited more from explicit support (Taylor et al., 2007).

In other words, how people communicate and receive care is culturally shaped, which makes the assumption that there is “one correct human way to empathize” highly dubious.

Yet this is precisely the standard that autistic people are held to when differences in how they express empathy are framed as “deficient.”

How Autistic Expressions of Empathy Can Be Misinterpreted

Autism is both a neurodevelopmental difference and, for many autistic people, the foundation of a shared culture. Autistic people have formed communities based on shared experiences, identities, communication styles, and ways of making meaning that scholars define as cultures (Botha et al., 2022; Davidson, 2008). How they express themselves, including how they show empathy, is shaped by both their neurological wiring and cultural learning.

To be clear: many autistic people can find it genuinely difficult to recognize or respond to what someone else is feeling, even when they care about them deeply. This may be especially true for autistic people with alexithymia, a difficulty identifying and describing emotions that is considerably more common in autistic than non-autistic (allistic) people (Kinnaird et al., 2019). But as Milton’s double empathy problem suggests, the difficulty may not be entirely one-sided, and non-autistic people may struggle with empathy toward autistic people (Milton, 2012).

Autistic people may express empathy in ways that don’t match non-autistic conventions. When others don’t recognize those differences, they may incorrectly assume that autistic people are indifferent to their feelings. Or, as some autism researchers have put it, autistic people may seem to lack empathy when they are simply following a different response script from the non-autistic majority (Fletcher-Watson & Bird, 2020).

An autistic person may hear about someone’s problem and immediately start looking for a solution. Conventional advice may call this “fixing instead of empathizing,” or “doing empathy wrong.” But the intended message may be: You are hurting; I want to help.

Someone may respond to a story with a similar experience of their own. This can be interpreted as “making it about yourself.” But it may just as easily mean: I understand. I have been in a similar situation too.

Other ways in which autistic people communicate can also be misconstrued. Providing detailed information can mean: I found something that might help you. Directness can communicate: I care enough to tell you what I actually think. And someone who becomes quiet during an emotionally intense interaction may not be indifferent; they may be overwhelmed and need time to process.

None of these behaviors is uniquely autistic, universal among autistic people, or interpreted in the same way by everyone. Problem-solving can be intrusive or welcome. Personal stories can derail a conversation or provide validation. Personal context and impact matter.

But so does cultural interpretation. When an autistic person’s ways of communicating are consistently misread, the consequences can extend far beyond a single interaction. An autistic employee may end up being labeled as “difficult” and passed over for promotion, when what looks like emotional insensitivity is actually a form of care, expressed as problem-solving.

For decades, autistic people have been measured by how well they recognize and respond to non-autistic social and emotional cues. A question we haven’t asked enough is: How well do non-autistic people recognize autistic expressions of empathy?

Rather than assuming that someone doesn’t care because their care arrived in an unfamiliar form, we can become curious about what that behavior means to them. We can ask what they were trying to communicate, rather than assuming we already know. We can leave room for the possibility that their intention was different from our interpretation. Equally, we can try to be more explicit about what kind of support is most helpful to us, instead of expecting the other person to guess.

Perhaps the ultimate test of empathy is recognizing that someone else may express it differently.

item.title: Let Your Desire Tell More Than One Story
item.description:
Sex

Let Your Desire Tell More Than One Story

Sexuality can be a space that allows competing stories to flourish.

Posted September 25, 2026

Hannah can describe her favorite fantasy without hesitation. Several men, all older than her, taking turns with one woman, in a scene that is rough and transgressive and stripped of any tenderness.

Then she describes her real life. She wants a partner close to her own age. She recoils from power imbalances in actual relationships, the kind where men seek much younger women. What she wants most is a lover who is patient and sweet, who prioritizes her pleasure and makes her feel safe.

Hannah cannot reconcile these two stories. If the fantasy is what arouses her most, she reasons, doesn’t that reflect what she actually wants, or worse, who she really is? She has started to wonder whether spending time in that fantasy makes her complicit in the very dynamics she has spent her adult life trying to avoid.

Multiple Scripts

Dan McAdams argues that we make sense of ourselves by building an internalized life story, one that gives us a sense of unity and purpose (McAdams & McLean, 2013). We are supposed to have one story. The version of us who wants tenderness and the version who wants danger are meant to resolve into a single, coherent account of who we are.

But that expectation is complicated the moment you look closely at anyone’s inner life. Researchers who study the self have found that people don’t always operate from one integrated narrative. Instead, the self behaves more like a cast of characters in dialogue with each other, each with its own logic, each active in a different context (Raggatt, 2006).

Sexuality tends to make this obvious in a way that daily life does not. Hannah’s fantasy self and Hannah’s relationship self are not in competition. They serve different purposes, each coming alive in its necessary context.

Why Desire Splits

Part of the answer is structural. Researchers who study attachment and desire have found evidence that our drive to feel safe and our drive to feel desire are not the same system, and they do not always want the same thing (Diamond, 2003). Attachment wants familiarity, safety, a nervous system at rest. Desire is often stirred by the opposite: novelty, intensity, a bit of danger. Hannah is not contradicting herself by wanting both. She is describing two different motivational systems doing what they were built to do.

Fantasy adds another layer. Sex researchers have repeatedly found that what people fantasize about and what they actually want to happen are only loosely related. Genital arousal and a person’s subjective sense of what turns them on often diverge, especially for women, suggesting that the body’s response to a scenario is not a straightforward yearning for that scenario in real life (Chivers et al., 2010). Studies of sexual fantasy content have found that scenes involving force, power, or taboo dynamics are common and are rarely a wish list for real experience (Lehmiller, 2018). A fantasy can be a place to feel something you would never choose for yourself.

Making More Room

Yet, none of this implies Hannah’s fantasy is meaningless. It means the fantasy is not a hidden confession waiting to be decoded. It is simply a room she visits, built for a specific kind of feeling, separate from the house she is building for her daily living.

The relief available to Hannah is not in choosing which self is the real one. It is in letting both exist without demanding they agree. The tender relationship she wants and the rough scene she craves are not competing verdicts on her character. They are two different stories, each serving its own purpose, doing the radical work of being allowed to exist alongside the other.

item.title: The Sculptor Who Fell in Love With an Illusion
item.description:
Parasocial Relationships

The Sculptor Who Fell in Love With an Illusion

Breaking the illusion and returning to the reality of authentic bonds.

Posted September 25, 2026

Fall is the perfect time to go within, refresh your routine, and engage your senses. Perhaps you take notice of the autumnal leaves, engage in novelty, or even travel. This change of season, this "newness," shatters the illusion that your current life is the only possible reality. Much like the myth of Pygmalion, we can easily lose touch with ourselves by getting caught up in the noise of this artificial world. This cautionary tale warns us of the heavy toll we pay—losing our identity and blurring healthy boundaries—when we let the noise of the world isolate us from our true selves.

The Story of Pygmalion

Pygmalion was a highly skilled and widely admired sculptor in Greek mythology. Disheartened by what he perceived as the imperfections of mortal women, he gave up pursuit of them and took a vow of celibacy. Instead, he dedicated himself to a life of art and creation and set out to create an artistic representation of the ideal female form. From the finest ivory, the sculptor devoted himself to chiseling every feature with increasing care and tenderness.

After many months, he transformed an already fine figure into one of unrivaled beauty—with refined features, radiant ivory skin, long windswept locks, and a generous waist-hip ratio. These visual signals of health and fertility remain timeless symbols of female beauty. He named his masterpiece Galatea. Once completed, the sculpture was so exquisitely beautiful that he fell deeply in love with it. The artwork was so lifelike that Pygmalion would touch it to confirm that it was not a living being. He progressed from admiring the sculpture to murmuring to it, caressing it, and even kissing it with his eyes closed. He envisioned her coming to life in his embrace. He was passionately in love with his own creation. He bestowed upon the statue gifts, dressed it in luxurious silks, undressed it, and even took it to bed.

According to the myth, Pygmalion prayed to the goddess Aphrodite on her festival day, his voice trembling with hope as he beseeched her to bring his beloved statue to life, longing for the warmth of a heartbeat and the spark of true love to awaken within the marble form he had crafted with such devotion. The Greek goddess of love, beauty, and desire was often described as charming, alluring, and enchanting. She was known for her irresistible beauty and her ability to inspire love and passion in others. Aphrodite was believed to embody love in all its forms, from romantic love to physical desire, and was associated with grace, elegance, and sensuality. When she encountered those truly devoted to love, she was known to show compassion, intervene, and even bestow blessings.

Pygmalion begged her to bring his beloved masterpiece to life, pleading for the “living likeness of my ivory girl." Aphrodite was moved by Pygmalion's pure and devoted love for Galatea. As a reward for his sincerity and passion, she brought the statue to life. When Pygmalion returned home, he kissed his beloved statue on the lips, as he always had. But this time, he was astonished to feel warmth and tenderness in the embrace. He could feel the pulse of sweet Galatea's lips as she began to return his kiss. The more he touched and caressed her, the more she came to life. Eventually, she opened her hazel eyes for the first time. Startled at first, she grew overjoyed by the sight of her devoted lover and reciprocated his ardor. With the blessing of Aphrodite, Pygmalion and Galatea were happily wed, and eventually they had a son.

Pygmalion had treated his statue like a real person. He spoke tenderly to Galatea, caressed her, and brought her thoughtful gifts. To him, she had become so much more than a statue carved from ivory; she became in his eyes the personification of the ideal woman. The myth has the couple living happily ever after. But in real life, Pygmalion's behavior would not lead to a happy ending.

Pygmalion's Fixation With Galatea Represents a Lack of Healthy Boundaries

Pygmalion lived in a trance, losing touch with the division between fantasy and reality. He put up emotional walls with real women that kept him in isolation; he lacked real emotional connection with the outer world, and clearly had difficulties in forming close relationships with real-life humans. His unrealistic ideals and disdain for women led him down the path of neglecting the need for authentic human connections. Many artists can empathize with this emotional journey of becoming so captivated by their creation that they immerse themselves in their inner world, forsaking the external world for the beauty of their imaginative ideals. This type of infatuation within the context of a "parasocial" relationship raises concerns about the dangers of losing touch with reality and getting lost in an illusion.

In today's world, a parasocial relationship is a one-sided, psychological bond that a lonely and isolated person may form with a media persona, celebrity, or public figure. In this type of relationship, the individual feels a sense of connection, attachment, or intimacy with the media personality, even though there is no actual interaction or personal relationship between them. This phenomenon is commonly observed in fandoms, where fans develop emotional connections with celebrities or characters they admire through media platforms like television, social media, or events. Parasocial relationships can have both positive and negative impacts on individuals, influencing their emotions, behaviors, and perceptions of the public figure involved. Ultimately, however, the relationship will feel hollow because it is inherently one-sided. The object of your affection isn't going to call you on your birthday or laugh with you about the smaller absurdities of life. The intimacy is an illusion.

In the age of AI, social media, and increased accessibility to celebrities, individuals can develop unrealistic expectations about their favorite personalities, leading to disappointment when those expectations are not met in reality. Parasocial relationships can allow people to connect without the risks associated with real-life interactions. They can offer a sense of vicarious companionship without the fear of real-life rejection or vulnerability. Emotional walls are constructed from bricks of self-protection and isolation, bound together by the cement of fear. They may create a mirage of safety, but ultimately relational trauma needs relational repair. One of the greatest psychological detriments of our time is the rise of parasocial relationships. This summer, take time to step into what is real.

And remember…

Individuals who understand the importance of boundaries are self-healers. Akin to alchemists, they possess the remarkable ability to transform wounds into wisdom, pain into purpose, and mistreatment from others into opportunities for assertive self-advocacy. This summer, I urge you to put down the phone and really connect with the person next to you. Forget the illusions of the online world. Say no to what feels parasocial and lean into those small nameless moments that are real.
